item.title: FBI Warns FortiBleed Campaign Still Active, Hits 86,000+ FortiGate Devices
item.description:
FortiBleed attacks continue to target Fortinet FortiGate devices, with SOCRadar reporting more than 86,644 compromised devices across 194 countries.

The FBI and US Secret Service are warning about ongoing FortiBleed attacks against internet-facing Fortinet FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPN gateways in a joint advisory (PDF) published on October 6, 2026.

Hackread.com first covered FortiBleed in June based on findings from Hudson Rock and researcher Volodymyr “Bob” Diachenko. The campaign was later linked to INC Ransom and Lynx ransomware activity, showing how exposed FortiGate access could move from credential abuse into ransomware operations.

SOCRadar has now shared additional findings with Hackread.com on the campaign’s infrastructure, credential-cracking operation and indicators.

According to the latest research, more than 86,644 devices across 194 countries have been compromised, with some victims finding themselves locked out after attackers changed passwords or removed existing accounts.

The latest advisory also identifies Payload ransomware among the groups connected to access obtained through the campaign.

How the FortiBleed Attacks Work

The campaign does not depend on a FortiOS zero-day. Attackers use credential stuffing (using stolen username-password pairs to try logging into other accounts) and password spraying (trying a few common passwords against many accounts) with credentials taken from previous Fortinet leaks and infostealer logs.

They then crack stolen password hashes offline using GPU-powered systems running Hashcat and Hashtopolis. Hashcat handles the password cracking, while Hashtopolis distributes the workload across multiple systems.

Legacy SHA-256 password storage in FortiOS made it easier for attackers to recover credentials from stolen hashes. After finding working credentials, they scan internet-facing Fortinet devices and use them to enter targeted networks.

On compromised devices, the attackers have also changed account settings. They can create new administrator accounts, delete existing ones or change passwords, leaving legitimate administrators unable to log in.

What Organizations Should Look For

SOCRadar found that the attackers use automated scripts to identify useful targets, filter out honeypots, and rank organizations based on factors such as revenue and network structure. After gaining access, they can enumerate Active Directory and look for accounts with higher privileges.

The advisory lists several suspicious administrator account names, including adminin, forticloud-tech, gttadmin, Technical_support, my_admin, forti_support2, and fgtsecure. These names should be checked against known accounts on affected FortiGate devices.

Organizations should also look at whether SSH was exposed and review REST API keys configured on the devices. An unauthorized API key can continue providing access even after passwords have been changed.

Steps for FortiGate Administrators

Resetting passwords is only one part of the cleanup. The advisory also calls for active administrator and VPN sessions to be terminated, Fortinet credentials to be reset, and management access from the internet to be restricted. Phishing-resistant multifactor authentication is recommended as an additional safeguard.

Fortinet administrators should check how their passwords are stored as well. The FBI and Secret Service recommend moving away from the older SHA-256 storage method and using PBKDF2 on supported FortiOS versions.

Where a compromise is confirmed, affected systems should be isolated and logs and other evidence reviewed before changes are made. The advisory also points organizations to CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool for help identifying and removing the attacker’s persistence.

Deeba Ahmed

item.title: Practical AI Integration for Modern Business Teams
item.description:
AI often gets introduced into a company before anyone has clearly defined what it should improve. A team tests a chatbot, another department experiments with automation, and management starts asking where the technology could reduce costs or speed up work. The tools may look promising, but that does not mean they fit the way the business actually operates.

The stronger starting point is usually much less glamorous. Look at repetitive tasks, slow handoffs, duplicated work, poor access to information, or decisions that take too long because employees have to gather data manually. AI becomes more useful when it is connected to one of those problems instead of being treated as a separate innovation project.

The Business Problem Comes Before the Model

Many weak AI projects begin with a tool rather than a need. Someone chooses a platform, sees what it can do, and then tries to find a place for it inside the company.

That sequence creates unnecessary work. Imagine a support department where agents spend a large part of the day reading incoming requests and deciding which team should handle them. The problem is not a lack of AI. The problem is the amount of manual sorting happening before useful work even begins.

In another company, sales representatives might spend fifteen minutes before every call searching through CRM notes, email history, and account activity. Operations teams may struggle to estimate demand because useful data sits in several systems.

Each situation points toward a different solution. None of them requires starting with the question, “Which AI model should we use?”

Friction Is Usually Easier to Find Than an AI Use Case

Employees already know which parts of their work are annoying. They know which reports require manual cleanup every week. They know which customer questions are repeated hundreds of times. They know when information is technically available but takes too long to find. Those moments are useful because they give an AI project something concrete to improve.

According to Avenga, an AI services company, projects involving several systems, custom development, or more complicated integration work often need the technical solution to be connected with existing business workflows. The important part is that the scope comes from the operational problem rather than from a desire to add AI somewhere. A narrow project can be more valuable than a large one if it removes something employees deal with every day.

AI Is Only as Useful as the Information Around It

A model can produce polished output while relying on poor information. That is one of the easiest risks to underestimate. An internal assistant may pull from product documentation, customer records, support tickets, pricing files, and internal policies. If some of those sources are outdated, the response can still sound confident even when it is wrong.

Forecasting systems have a similar weakness. Historical data may contain gaps, inconsistent categories, or unusual periods that are never explained. Customer information may be duplicated across different platforms. One department can use a definition that another team interprets differently.

The AI layer does not remove those inconsistencies. It often makes them harder to see because the result arrives in a cleaner form. Before building more automation, companies may need to fix very ordinary issues such as naming, access, ownership, and data freshness.

Automation Should Remove Steps, Not Rearrange Them

Some AI systems look efficient until the real workflow is examined. An employee receives an automated summary, checks it against the original document, corrects several details, copies the result into another platform, and then updates the source record manually. The company has technically added automation, but the person still performs most of the process.

That is not always a model problem. It can be an integration problem. Connecting tools through a well-planned marketing automation integration can remove manual transfers between systems instead of simply moving them to another part of the workflow.

Human review makes sense when a decision carries financial, legal, or customer risk. It makes less sense when a person is forced to approve routine output because the surrounding systems do not communicate properly. A useful design asks where human judgment adds value and where it simply adds another click.

Where AI Can Save Time Without Creating Extra Noise

The most practical applications are often small enough to sound ordinary. That is usually a good sign. AI may help when teams face repetitive work such as:

  • Support teams sorting the same types of requests every day. A system can classify tickets, detect urgency, and send each request to the right queue before an agent opens it.
  • Salespeople preparing for customer calls. Instead of opening several systems, they can receive a short account summary built from recent activity, CRM notes, and previous conversations.
  • Operations teams watching large amounts of changing data. Unusual demand, inventory movement, or transaction behavior can be flagged without someone checking every number manually.
  • Employees searching through internal documentation. A connected assistant can surface relevant policies, project notes, or technical information without forcing people to remember the folder structure.
  • Finance and administration processing similar documents. Forms, invoices, and reports can be categorized or summarized before a person reviews the details that actually require attention.

For teams dealing specifically with lead routing, qualification, CRM updates, and follow-up, lead management automation is another example of how repetitive steps can be handled without adding more manual work.

The value depends on frequency. Saving two minutes on a task performed once a month means very little. Saving two minutes on something that happens hundreds of times a day is different.

Trust Usually Breaks Before the Technology Does

A technically working AI system can still fail because employees stop using it. That often happens after a few bad experiences.

A sales rep sees an incorrect account summary and starts checking everything manually. A support agent receives several weak suggested responses and goes back to writing from scratch. A manager gets a recommendation with no explanation and ignores it because there is no way to understand what influenced the result.

People do not need a detailed explanation of the model architecture. They do need enough context to judge whether the output deserves attention.

That can mean showing the source behind an answer, indicating which data influenced a recommendation, or making uncertainty visible instead of presenting every result with the same level of confidence. The interface matters here as much as the model.

Small AI Projects Often Expose Bigger Problems

A limited AI pilot can reveal issues that have nothing to do with AI itself. A company building an internal search assistant may discover that nobody owns half of its documentation. A forecasting project can uncover three different definitions of the same sales metric. A customer service tool may reveal duplicate accounts spread across several systems.

Those problems were already there. The AI project simply creates a reason to inspect them. This is one reason smaller implementations can be useful before a broader rollout. They show how data, permissions, processes, and technical systems behave when they are forced to work together.

A pilot may also reveal that the company does not need AI for part of the workflow at all. A cleaner integration or a simpler automation can sometimes solve the same issue with less maintenance.

Existing Systems Matter More Than the Demo

AI demonstrations usually happen in controlled environments. Real businesses are not controlled environments.

Customer records contain incomplete fields. Employees enter information differently. Integrations fail. Old products remain in databases. Regional teams create their own processes because the central system does not fit local work.

An AI tool has to operate inside that reality. That is why integration work often matters more than the model itself. The system may need access to CRM data, internal documents, support history, analytics platforms, or custom applications. Permissions must follow existing responsibilities, and the output has to appear somewhere employees will actually use it. If the AI tool lives in a separate tab that nobody opens, even accurate output can become irrelevant.

AI Systems Change When the Business Changes

A useful AI setup is not static. A company launches a new product, and suddenly the assistant needs different documentation. A sales team enters another market and the patterns behind lead scoring change. New privacy requirements affect which information can be processed. Customer behavior shifts enough that an old forecasting model starts missing patterns it once captured.

The system may still be running normally while becoming less useful. That creates a maintenance problem that is easy to ignore. Teams need to review source data, integrations, permissions, model behavior, and the original purpose of the project from time to time. A system built around real business work has to keep moving with that work.

item.title: MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi Accused of Paying Hackers, Defrauding Victims
item.description:
The DOJ accuses MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi of secretly paying ransomware gangs for decryption keys while charging victims hefty recovery fees.

Zohar Pinhasi, owner of Florida-based ransomware recovery firm MonsterCloud LLC, faces federal charges over allegations that he misled businesses about how the company recovered encrypted data. Pinhasi, who also used the names Zack Silver and Zack Green, appeared in federal court in Brooklyn on October 7 to face charges over his company’s ransomware recovery services.

According to the indictment (PDF), Pinhasi claimed MonsterCloud could recover encrypted files without paying a ransom. Prosecutors allege he instead paid the attackers for decryption keys and charged clients much higher fees.

Pinhasi faces two wire fraud charges and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud. If convicted on all three counts, he could face a maximum of 60 years in prison, with each count carrying a potential sentence of up to 20 years.

Earlier Scrutiny of MonsterCloud

The charges also create an unusual link to Hackread.com’s own archive. In February 2019, Hackread.com published a ransomware prevention article written by Pinhasi as a guest author in his capacity as MonsterCloud’s CEO. In that article, he warned readers about ransomware risks and discussed ways to protect systems from attacks.

Pinhasi’s author profile on Hackread.com described him as an ethical hacker, cyber counter-cyberterrorism expert, ransomware recovery expert, former IT security intelligence officer for the Israeli military and CEO of MonsterCloud, with more than 25 years of cybersecurity and enterprise IT experience.

Pinhasi also appeared in earlier public interviews discussing ransomware recovery and MonsterCloud’s work, including a 2019 video interview in which he spoke about ransomware incidents, recovery services and victim response.

Later that same year, ProPublica investigated MonsterCloud and other recovery firms that advertised their ability to restore encrypted files. The investigation found that MonsterCloud paid ransomware attackers in some cases, sometimes without telling clients.

The US Department of Justice (DOJ) now alleges that Pinhasi claimed to have proprietary decryption technology when, in fact, he paid attackers for decryption keys. The indictment also cites a May 2019 exchange in which an allegedly paid MonsterCloud spokesperson asked Pinhasi whether the company had proprietary decryption software. Pinhasi allegedly replied that it did not.

Secret Payments and Inflated Fees

According to the DoJ’s press release, MonsterCloud claimed it could recover data using proprietary tools and advanced decryption techniques. Pinhasi allegedly lacked specialized technology to decrypt the affected files and instead contacted the attackers for decryption keys, which employees then used in attempts to recover clients’ files.

In August 2023, Pinhasi allegedly paid a ransomware attacker $8,200 and charged the customer $150,000. In a separate case, he allegedly paid $236,000 but billed the customer $380,000. According to the indictment, he charged clients more than $19 million and paid over $8 million to attackers.

“As alleged, Zohar Pinhasi claimed to fix ransomware while never remediating the underlying threat. Instead, he turned the victim’s crisis into his own profit center,” said FBI Assistant Director James C. Barnacle Jr. “This deception is unacceptable, and the FBI is committed to ensuring accountability for those who choose to victimize the very people who trusted them for help.”

The FBI and CISA advise against paying ransoms (PDF), as payment does not guarantee that files will be recovered or that stolen data will not be leaked. The FBI is investigating the case. Although Pinhasi has been charged but is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

item.title: FBI Arrests Ransomware Negotiation Firm Co-Founder in ShinyHunters Probe
item.description:
FBI arrests Cypfer co-founder Edward Dubrovsky, now associated with CyberSteward, in the ShinyHunters investigation into the FBI jobs portal breach.

A co-founder of Canadian ransomware negotiation firm Cypfer has been identified as the person arrested in connection with the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation, adding an unexpected turn to a case already involving suspected hackers, breached FBI systems and international arrests.

The New York Times reported on October 9 that the FBI had arrested a suspect in Pennsylvania connected to the ShinyHunters investigation. Cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs later identified the suspect as Edward Dubrovsky, a Canadian cybersecurity executive and co-founder of Cypfer. Krebs reported that Dubrovsky is now associated with another Canadian security firm, CyberSteward.

Dubrovsky is not an unknown figure in cybersecurity. His professional background is in ransomware negotiation and incident response, work normally associated with helping companies respond to extortion attacks.

The arrest also comes days after a separate DOJ case against MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, another ransomware recovery figure accused of secretly paying attackers for decryption keys while charging victims higher recovery fees. The two cases are separate, but both put new scrutiny on companies and individuals working around ransomware recovery and negotiation.

The FBI has not publicly released Dubrovsky’s name in a formal announcement reviewed by Hackread.com. The exact charges, if any, and his alleged role in the ShinyHunters investigation were not immediately clear at the time of writing.

Court records reviewed by Hackread.com show the case was filed in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania on October 8 and terminated there on October 9 after Dubrovsky was committed to the Eastern District of Texas. A bail status order says the government moved for detention, the motion was granted, and Dubrovsky was detained pending a detention hearing in the charging district.

New Arrest Follows Rey Detention

The reported arrest follows earlier coverage of suspected ShinyHunters member Saif al-Din Khader, known online as “Rey,” who was detained in Jordan on September 29. Reuters reported that Khader was cooperating with the FBI and other authorities as investigators worked to identify others connected to the group.

Hackread.com also reported that the FBI confirmed multiple arrests in the ShinyHunters investigation, but declined to identify all suspects or confirm whether Khader was among them. At the time, the bureau said it was working with international partners and continuing to pursue people involved in the cyber incident.

The FBI’s investigation intensified after ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for compromising the FBI’s job application portal (apply.fbijobs.gov).

The group claimed it accessed sensitive information belonging to current, former and prospective FBI personnel, including personal and health-related data. Days later, ShinyHunters told Hackread.com that it will not leak the stolen FBI data and that the breach was part of its marketing campaign.

The FBI confirmed unauthorized activity affecting the jobs portal but has not publicly verified ShinyHunters’ full claims about the stolen data.

PeopleSoft Breach and Contractor Fallout

The FBI jobs portal incident has also led to fallout around third-party system management. A missed security patch reportedly left the bureau’s Oracle PeopleSoft jobs portal exposed, leading the FBI to remove a contractor from its assignment. Accenture was identified as the company managing the platform.

ShinyHunters previously claimed it exploited a PeopleSoft vulnerability to gain access. Google’s Mandiant separately reported that the group had exploited CVE-2026-35273, a critical flaw in Oracle PeopleSoft’s Environment Management component, and used URL encoding to get around WAF rules blocking the vulnerable endpoint.

The newly reported arrest adds another piece to a fast-moving investigation, but several details remain unresolved. item.title: Dark Web Empire Market Co-Creator Raheim Hamilton Gets 40 Years in Prison
item.description:
Raheim Hamilton, co-creator of the dark web marketplace Empire Market, was sentenced to 40 years for a platform that handled $430M in illegal sales.

Raheim Hamilton, co-creator of the dark web marketplace Empire Market, has been sentenced to 40 years in federal prison for helping operate a platform that processed more than $430 million in illegal transactions.

The US Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Illinois said Hamilton, 30, of Suffolk, Virginia, co-owned and operated Empire Market from 2018 to 2020. He pleaded guilty earlier this year in federal court in Chicago to a drug conspiracy charge.

Empire Market allowed vendors and buyers to trade illegal goods and services, including controlled substances, stolen account credentials, stolen personally identifiable information, counterfeit currency and hacking tools. Prosecutors said the site handled more than four million transactions during its operation.

According to the Justice Department, drug sales made up most of the marketplace’s activity, with net drug sales reaching nearly $375 million and including fentanyl, cocaine, methamphetamine and heroin.

Hamilton and co-creator Thomas Pavey designed the platform to help users avoid law enforcement detection. The platform used cryptocurrency to carry out transactions and users were encouraged to use tumbling and mixing services to conceal payments.

The site also supported encrypted communications and allowed buyers to rate vendors on how well they concealed drugs shipped through the mail. Empire Market operated from 2018 until 2020, when it disappeared from the dark web, prompting speculation at the time that it may have been an exit scam. The Justice Department’s sentencing announcement does not describe the site as having been seized by law enforcement.

US District Judge Steven C. Seeger sentenced Hamilton on Monday and imposed a $5 million fine. Hamilton also agreed to forfeit proceeds linked to the marketplace, including about 1,230 bitcoin, 24.4 Ether and three properties in Virginia.

On the other hand, Pavey, 41, of Ormond Beach, Florida, pleaded guilty last year to a federal drug conspiracy charge and admitted his role in creating and operating Empire Market. He agreed to forfeit about 1,584 bitcoin, two boxes containing 25-ounce gold bars, three vehicles, and two Florida properties. His sentencing is scheduled for later this month.

item.title: Hackers Heat Supermarket Fridges to 50°C in France Cyberattack
item.description:
Hackers reportedly heated supermarket fridges to 50°C in France, spoiling food stocks, while stores in the Netherlands and Belgium faced separate IT outages.

Supermarkets in France are dealing with large food losses after a cyberattack reportedly targeted refrigeration-control systems and forced equipment to heat instead of keeping products cold.

According to French reporting citing BFMTV, the attack began overnight from Sunday to Monday and affected refrigeration systems linked to Danish manufacturer Danfoss. The unknown attackers reportedly abused the defrosting function in older control software, setting some equipment to heat continuously, with temperatures said to have reached 50°C.

The cyber attack impacted several major supermarket chains, including Intermarché, Super U and E.Leclerc. Metro stores and smaller independent businesses, including butcher shops, were also reported to have been hit.

French outlets including Clubic, 01net and Capital reported that around 150 Intermarché stores may have been affected. The total number of affected locations has not yet been confirmed.

Stores Forced to Throw Away Food

The impact was visible quickly because the cyberattack hit systems used to preserve fresh and frozen products. Once the cold chain was broken, stores had to discard goods rather than risk selling unsafe food.

In Haguenau, Alsace, an Intermarché store reportedly lost its frozen-food stock, worth about €50,000. A nearby Super U reportedly discarded both fresh and frozen products, with losses estimated at about €220,000. An E.Leclerc store in the same town was also affected, although its losses had not been calculated at the time of reporting.

The confirmed losses from the two Haguenau stores alone were reported at about €270,000. If the number of affected stores is confirmed, the total damage could reach several million euros.

Coopérative U acknowledged that refrigeration installations in several stores had been affected and said teams were working with refrigeration specialists to restore service. Intermarché also reportedly warned internally that several stores had lost frozen products.

Danfoss Systems Named in Reports

The reported target was not supermarket payment systems, customer accounts or e-commerce sites, but equipment used to control refrigeration.

Refrigeration-control software can manage cooling, temperature settings and defrost cycles. A defrost cycle is normally a controlled process used to prevent ice buildup, but the reports say attackers manipulated that function so equipment heated for far longer than intended.

Danfoss has been named in French reporting as the supplier of the affected refrigeration-control systems. At the time of writing, the reports reviewed by Hackread.com did not include a public statement from Danfoss confirming the technical cause or naming the affected software versions.

The identity of the attackers has also not been confirmed. It is also unclear whether the attack involved exposed remote access, compromised credentials, unpatched vulnerabilities, or another route into the control systems.

Dutch Retailer Reports Separate Cybersecurity Incident

A separate retail disruption is also affecting Ahold Delhaize brands in the Netherlands and Belgium, although no public evidence currently links it to the French refrigeration attack.

Dutch public broadcaster NOS reported that Albert Heijn, Etos and Gall & Gall have suffered disruption since Sunday afternoon after what parent company Ahold Delhaize described as a “cybersecurity incident.” Albert Heijn had earlier referred to it as an IT incident.

The disruption was not limited to store systems. Albert Heijn’s websites, apps and customer service were unavailable, online grocery deliveries were paused, loyalty systems stopped working and some electronic shelf labels still showed last week’s promotional prices. Delhaize in Belgium also reported problems, with customers unable to place new online orders or reach customer service.

Ahold Delhaize said it had taken immediate measures to protect its IT environment, including temporarily switching off some systems as a precaution. The company said it was investigating the incident and working to restore services, with protection of customer, employee and partner data as a priority.

For now, the French refrigeration attack and the Ahold Delhaize disruption should be treated as separate incidents unless investigators or the companies say otherwise.

item.title: Why Robust VPS Hosting Helps OpenClaw Run Faster and More Reliably
item.description:
OpenClaw is not a chatbot that waits for a prompt. It is an autonomous agent that runs real computer tasks, remembers what it has done, and stays connected to the messaging apps you already use, all day and all night.

That kind of nonstop work asks a lot of the machine underneath it. Run it on a shared box or a home computer and the cracks can show fast. Put it on a strong virtual private server, and the experience becomes faster, steadier, and easier to rely on.

The reason is simple: an agent that never sleeps needs resources that are always available. Here is how robust hosting removes the limits that can hold OpenClaw back.

Why an Autonomous Agent Is So Demanding

Before looking at hardware, it helps to understand what the agent is doing behind the scenes, because that workload is heavier than it first appears.

It Runs Nonstop, Not on Request

A normal app answers a request and goes quiet. OpenClaw works differently. It keeps a process running around the clock, holding on to context, user preferences, and project states so nothing resets between sessions. At the same time, it can juggle scheduled jobs, read files, and run commands in the background.

All of that needs memory and processing power that stay available, not resources that disappear when another user on a shared server gets busy. When those resources drop at the wrong moment, a scheduled job can fail, a task can slow down, or the agent can fall behind on work you expected it to handle.

It Works Beyond the Chat Window

The agent does more than send messages. It can open web pages, work through them, extract the data you asked for, and act on what it finds. On a personal laptop, that browser activity competes with everything else running on the machine and can quickly slow things down.

On a dedicated server, the same work happens separately from your day-to-day device. That means OpenClaw can keep working in the background without dragging down your laptop or interrupting other tasks. With fewer local limits, jobs finish faster and results are more consistent.

Hardware That Clears the Bottlenecks

Once you understand that the agent runs hard and never stops, the value of stronger hardware becomes clear. Each part of the server removes a different drag on performance.

Fast Storage and Enough Memory

Speed starts with storage. Fast solid-state drives help the agent retrieve saved context, files, and database lookups quickly, so tasks do not stall midway. Memory matters just as much. A robust VPS gives OpenClaw enough RAM to run several workflows at once and handle larger workloads without choking.

That extra headroom also matters as you add skills, integrations, and background jobs. Each one draws from the same pool of memory. If the server is already stretched, performance drops. If there is room to work, the agent stays responsive even when the workload grows.

Dedicated Processing Power

Shared hosting splits processor time and memory across many users. That means your agent can slow down whenever another account on the same machine starts using more resources. For an always-on autonomous agent, that inconsistency creates problems.

Using VPS hosting for OpenClaw gives the agent more consistent compute resources, so heavier scripts, browser tasks, and multi-step reasoning can run more steadily. The exact performance gain depends on the workload, server configuration, and how OpenClaw is set up, but dedicated resources give the system a much stronger foundation.

Stable Network and Uptime

Strong hardware only helps if the agent can be reached and can reach external services reliably. That is where the network side matters.

Awake and Responsive Around the Clock

A home or office connection was never built to host an always-on agent. Devices sleep, IP addresses can change, and bandwidth can run thin when other activity picks up. A server in a professional data center stays online even when your own devices are turned off.

Hosting closer to users can also reduce response times for webhooks and API calls. Better bandwidth helps with steady web work, file transfers, and background tasks, so the agent does not get stuck waiting on a weak connection. The result is simple: OpenClaw is more likely to respond when it is needed, instead of waiting for the network to recover.

Built to Keep Running

Consistent uptime becomes important when a business starts depending on the agent. If the server behind it keeps running, the work it supports keeps moving with fewer gaps. That reliability also makes it easier to plan for backups, recovery, monitoring, and other steps that keep operations steady if something goes wrong.

Robust hosting does not remove the need for proper configuration, security, and maintenance, but it gives OpenClaw a more dependable base to run from.

Conclusion

Robust VPS hosting does not just keep OpenClaw online. It helps the agent perform the way it was designed to. Fast storage, enough memory, dedicated compute, and a stable network each improve a different part of the workload. Together, they can turn a slow or unreliable setup into one that responds faster and runs more consistently.

For anyone relying on an autonomous agent to handle real work, the server underneath is not a minor detail. It is one of the main factors that decides how well everything else runs.

item.title: G2A.COM Reports 35% Growth in Security Software Orders, Outpacing VPN Growth
item.description:
Amsterdam, Netherlands, October 13th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Antivirus and security software orders grow more than twice as fast as VPN orders, accounting for 43% of cybersecurity purchases on the marketplace 

G2A.COM, a digital marketplace that serves more than 35 million users across 180 countries, reports a 35% year-on-year surge in antivirus and security software orders, outpacing VPN orders.   

Released during Cybersecurity Awareness Month, the marketplace figures reveal that security software accounted for 43% of cybersecurity-related orders during the period, up from 39% in the equivalent period in 2025. Overall, orders across cybersecurity products increased by almost a quarter (24%).  

VPNs remain the larger category, but antivirus and security software are taking a greater share of purchases on G2A.COM. The findings highlight that consumers are increasingly looking beyond privacy and secure connectivity towards broader protection of their devices, accounts and digital activity 

The trend comes as the global cyber threat landscape continues to evolve. According to the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) Threat Landscape 2026, ransomware remains the most impactful type of cyber incident in the short term, while social engineering continues to be widely used to exploit trust.  

“What we’re seeing is a shift from privacy-first protection towards a more layered approach to cybersecurity” said Adrian Podkaminer, Chief Information Security Officer at G2A.COM. “As people move between more devices, accounts and digital services, effective cybersecurity increasingly depends on different safeguards working together rather than relying on a single solution.” 

G2A.COM marketplace data suggests that consumers are taking a more active approach to protecting their digital lives. At the same time, they do not see security as their responsibility alone. According to the Trust in Digital Commerce report, a survey by G2A.COM and Juniper Research involving 9,000 consumers from nine countries found that half of them think e-commerce sites are mainly responsible for security. Meanwhile, a third blame banks and payment providers, and 20% say it’s up to the consumers themselves. 

For G2A.COM, that responsibility translates into concrete safeguards. The marketplace works exclusively with verified business sellers and applies KYC, KYB and AML processes, supported by AI-based fraud prevention and continuous monitoring. 

Cybersecurity Awareness Month offers an opportunity for consumers to review both the tools they use and the habits that help protect their accounts. G2A.COM encourages users to: 

  • Secure important accounts: use strong, unique passwords and enable multi-factor authentication wherever available, particularly for email, shopping and payment accounts. 
  • Keep devices updated: install operating system, browser and application updates promptly. 
  • Check before clicking: treat unexpected login requests, downloads and urgent payment messages cautiously, and visit the official website or app directly. 
  • Understand the protection purchased: check what a security product covers, its compatibility with existing devices and any subscription or renewal terms. 

About G2A.COM 

G2A.COM is the world’s largest marketplace for digital entertainment, serving over 35 million users from 180 countries with more than 200 million visits in 2025. As a true gateway to digital entertainment and a rapidly evolving digital ecosystem, G2A.COM gives access to over 125,000 digital offerings, including vouchers, games, DLCs, in-game items, and non-gaming items such as gift cards, subscriptions, software, or e-learning, sold by sellers from all over the world. A compliance-driven organization audited by Deloitte for over a decade, G2A.COM is a leader in online security, recognized by the prestigious American CNP Award alongside industry giants like Microsoft and PayPal. Today, the company is a key gateway for recognized global brands, leveraging its scalable infrastructure to drive the next phase of e-commerce through agentic AI and global M&A – continuously expanding its role as the Gate 2 Adventure in the digital world.

item.title: Amazon Fire TV Cube Rooted Using Four-Year-Old Arm Mali Vulnerability
item.description:
A four-year-old Arm Mali GPU vulnerability can be used to root the third-generation Amazon Fire TV Cube, but its patch status remains unclear.

A vulnerability in Arm’s Mali GPU driver, first disclosed four years ago, has been adapted to gain root access to the third-generation Amazon Fire TV Cube, allowing users to remove Amazon’s software restrictions and install alternative operating systems, according to Cybernews research shared with Hackread.com.

The exploit uses CVE-2022-38181 (CVSS 8.8), a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in the Arm Mali GPU kernel driver. The bug involves memory that the driver frees while it may still be in use, creating an opportunity to manipulate kernel memory and gain elevated privileges.

Security researcher Man Yue Mo reported the vulnerability to the Android security team on July 12, 2022. His original proof of concept showed how an unprivileged Android process could exploit the bug to execute code in the kernel and gain root access on a Google Pixel 6.

What the Fire TV Cube Exploit Allows

Mo’s technical write-up explains that the process can trigger memory pressure through standard system calls, prompting the driver to free active Just-In-Time (JIT) memory allocations. By manipulating how the kernel reuses that memory, the process can overwrite internal driver structures and take control of kernel space, ultimately gaining root privileges.

Arm released a fix in Mali driver version r40p0 on October 7, 2022. The third-generation Fire TV Cube launched on October 25 that year, but it remains unclear whether Amazon incorporated the fix into FireOS or whether the vulnerable driver remained present on the device.

What Root Access Lets Users Do

Later, a developer using the alias Pro-me3us shared an adapted version of the exploit on XDA Forums, making it work with FireOS’s 32-bit userspace. With root access, users can install Magisk, replace the Fire TV Cube’s stock recovery system, and load other operating systems.

These include CoreELEC, a Linux-based system built around Kodi for media playback, and EmuELEC, which focuses on retro gaming. Both give users alternatives to Amazon’s standard software, particularly those who want to play local media files or run games on the device.

“For casual Netflix viewers, this might not mean much, but it’s very important for home theater enthusiasts with multi-channel audio setups and the itch to see the content at maximum quality, as the creators intended,” Cybernews noted.

Amazon Says Physical Access Is Required

Amazon told Cybernews that the demonstrated method poses little risk to customers because it requires physical access and deliberate, multiple-step modifications.

“Protecting the security of our customers and devices is our top priority,” an Amazon spokesperson said. “What’s being demonstrated poses little risk to customers; it’s someone modifying a device they own to run unofficial software, which requires direct physical access and a deliberate, multi-step process.”

Since the exploit requires code to run on the device first, the vulnerability alone does not put every Fire TV Cube owner at immediate risk. However, root access could expose data or allow further malicious activity if abused. Cybernews reported no evidence that the exploit was being used in real-world attacks.

Amazon has yet to confirm whether CVE-2022-38181 has been patched in the Fire TV Cube. Until the device’s patch status is clarified, users should be cautious about modifying the system or installing unofficial software.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: Powering Proactive Defense: How MSSPs Can Strengthen Threat Hunting Against Ransomware
item.description:
Ransomware defense cannot rely on alerts alone. For MSSPs in particular, the ability to proactively hunt for attacker infrastructure and emerging campaigns can mean finding threats before they become major incidents.

Threat intelligence feeds give security teams a way to make threat hunting more continuous and scalable. By feeding fresh, actionable intelligence into the solutions analysts already use, they can turn external threat activity into concrete hunting opportunities across customer environments.

The Role of Threat Hunting in Modern MSSP Security

Threat hunting gives MSSPs a proactive way to identify suspicious activity that may not trigger existing detections.

Customers expect their security provider to identify threats before they result in disruption, data loss, or costly incident response. That means an MSSP team needs to do more than respond to alerts generated by individual customer environments. It has to understand what attackers are doing outside those environments and use that intelligence to look for relevant activity inside them.

Ransomware makes this especially important. By the time encryption is detected, an attacker may have already gained access, established persistence, moved laterally, or stolen sensitive data.

Recent research into IronChain illustrates how quickly ransomware can turn into a broader business continuity problem. The September 2026 build analyzed in ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox combined destructive file handling with SYSTEM-level persistence and multiple kernel drivers, creating several points that defenders could investigate before or during an incident. 

The research also found that the malware’s encryption design may leave affected files without a reliable recovery path, increasing the potential impact of an attack.

Proactive hunting allows security teams to search for earlier signs of compromise. The challenge is scale. An MSSP may be responsible for dozens or hundreds of environments, each generating large amounts of telemetry. Asking analysts to manually collect indicators, research campaigns, build queries, and validate findings for every customer quickly becomes expensive and difficult to sustain.

Threat intelligence helps address this challenge by giving security teams the insight they need to identify emerging threats and focus their hunting efforts. 

Turning Threat Intelligence Feeds into a Hunting Engine

Threat intelligence feeds should not simply add more indicators to an MSSP’s database. Their value comes from helping analysts identify what to hunt for, where to look, and which findings deserve attention.

ANY.RUN’s Threat Intelligence Feeds (TI Feeds) provide continuously updated malicious IPs, domains, and URLs enriched with sandbox analysis. Their quality is supported by millions of sandbox investigations, with contributions from more than 700,000 analysts and activity from over 16,000 organizations. 

That scale gives MSSPs a broader pool of threat intelligence to support hunting across customer environments.

Feeds can be integrated into SIEM, EDR, XDR, SOAR, firewalls, and other security technologies. Through connectors, API/SDK, and STIX/TAXII, intelligence can flow into the systems where analysts are already investigating customer environments.

Consider a ransomware group that starts using new command-and-control infrastructure. Without external intelligence, an MSSP may only investigate that infrastructure after an internal alert or customer incident brings it to their attention.

With an intelligence-driven hunting model, the indicators can become hunting leads first. Analysts can search customer telemetry for connections to the infrastructure, investigate related activity, and determine whether other environments show signs of the same campaign.

Get 99% unique, high-confidence IOCs to strengthen your threat detection.

IronChain provides a practical example of why this approach matters. A newly observed build can introduce fresh hashes, dropped components, persistence mechanisms, and other behavioral artifacts. Instead of treating the malware sample as an isolated incident, an MSSP can use those findings to search across customer environments for related activity, such as unexpected drivers, privileged scheduled tasks, or other indicators associated with the same threat.

The question shifts from “Did we detect an attack?” to “Where could this attack already be present?” That distinction is particularly valuable for MSSPs because a single piece of intelligence can inform hunts across multiple customer environments.

Making Threat Hunting More Scalable

The value of threat intelligence should ultimately be measured by its impact on processes within a security team, not by the number of indicators in a feed.

High-quality intelligence can reduce the manual work involved in collecting, validating, and maintaining IOCs. That gives analysts more time to investigate meaningful activity instead of spending their time preparing the data needed to investigate it.

MSSP teams that use ANY.RUN’s solutions report a 50% reduction in IOC extraction time, 94% of users reporting faster triage, and up to 3x better SOC performance.

For team leaders, these outcomes matter more than the sheer volume of indicators a feed delivers. Faster investigations and lower analyst workload can translate into greater customer coverage without requiring a proportional increase in headcount.

That creates a direct connection between threat intelligence and the economics of delivering managed security services.

Feeds Provide the Scale, Context Makes Them Useful

An indicator rarely tells everything an MSSP team needs to know. If a customer’s endpoint connects to an IP listed in a threat intelligence feed, the analyst still needs to establish why the connection matters. What malware used the infrastructure? Is the IP associated with other domains or files? What behaviors have been observed? Is the activity part of a known campaign?

An integrated intelligence ecosystem can provide much more value than a standalone feed.

For example, ANY.RUN’s Threat Intelligence Lookup (TI Lookup) allows analysts to investigate indicators and pivot through related threat data, including IPs, domains, URLs, hashes, files, processes, signatures, YARA rules, and TTPs.

Threat hunters can use a feed match to launch a deeper investigation into the associated activity. Instead of treating an IP address as an isolated artifact, they can investigate its relationships with malware, infrastructure, behaviors, and previous sandbox activity. That context can reveal additional indicators and hunting opportunities that would otherwise be easy to miss.

ANY.RUN’s Threat Intelligence Reports (TI Reports) add another layer of context by connecting individual indicators to broader campaigns, threat actors, and attack techniques. 

This helps MSSPs understand the bigger picture behind a feed match and identify new hunting opportunities before related activity appears across customer environments.

Detect up to 58% more threats with intelligence built for faster, broader coverage.

Using Interactive Sandbox Analysis to Accelerate Investigations

Threat hunting often raises questions that an IOC alone can’t answer.

An MSSP may discover a suspicious file in a customer environment or encounter an unfamiliar payload connected to an emerging campaign. Understanding what that file actually does can determine whether the finding represents a genuine threat and what the analyst should hunt for next.

ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox provides an environment for analyzing suspicious files and URLs and observing their behavior. In 90% of cases, threats become visible within 60 seconds of analysis, helping organizations achieve a reported 36% increase in threat detection.

The IronChain investigation shows how behavioral analysis can add useful context to a ransomware sample. The public sandbox session exposed the process tree, network activity, dropped files, and system changes, while the broader analysis connected those observations with persistence, driver activity, and attempts to impair security controls.

Sandboxing also helps turn technical analysis into information that analysts can act on more quickly. Tier 1 Reports summarize malware behavior in an analyst-friendly format, while AI Summary condenses execution activity into key findings and attack stages. AI Recommendations can then point analysts toward additional artifacts, indicators, and behaviors worth investigating.

This can reduce the analyst time required to move from a suspicious artifact to a useful hunting hypothesis.

More importantly, sandbox analysis can feed the broader intelligence workflow. A newly observed malware sample can reveal infrastructure and behaviors that become new hunting leads, creating a continuous feedback loop between investigation and threat intelligence.

The Business Value of Intelligence-Driven Hunting

For CISOs and SOC leaders, the business case for threat intelligence should come down to a few practical questions. Does it help the team find threats earlier? Does it reduce investigation time? Can analysts cover more environments without increasing workload at the same rate? Does it improve the quality of customer outcomes?

Those questions are particularly important in an MSSP environment, where operational efficiency directly affects the ability to scale.

An intelligence-driven hunting program can help reduce manual IOC collection, improve investigation prioritization, and give analysts more context when they encounter suspicious activity. The result can be faster threat discovery, shorter response times, and better use of scarce security expertise.

The customer-facing value is equally important. An MSSP that can demonstrate proactive hunting based on current threat intelligence can offer something beyond reactive monitoring: evidence that its security team is actively looking for threats relevant to the customer’s environment.

That can become a meaningful differentiator in a crowded managed security market.

Cut 21 minutes from MTTR and accelerate threat response across every client.

Speed Up MSSP Response

Conclusion

The value of threat intelligence comes from how effectively it can be turned into proactive security action. Threat intelligence feeds provide a continuous flow of actionable indicators, while investigation, analysis, and threat research add the context analysts need to understand threats and prioritize hunting efforts.

This connected approach can help MSSPs scale proactive hunting, enabling SOC teams to identify threats earlier, respond faster, and use analyst resources more effectively across customer environments.

Ransomware will keep evolving, but MSSPs that turn fresh intelligence into targeted, continuous hunting can strengthen defenses while delivering greater value to customers.
